caption:
UC Berkeley math professor and Fields Medal winner Richard Borcherds no longer grades homework for correctness.
After seeing many students use AI to earn top scores, he now gives credit just for turning it in.
He also says he has no idea what to advise students who want to become mathematicians.

Should colleges stop grading homework altogether?

paragraphs.text: Richard Borcherds, a mathematics professor at UC Berkeley and a winner of the Fields Medal, has stopped grading his students' homework for correctness, according to an interview published by The Daily Californian on October 23, 2026. He now gives credit to students who turn in their assignments, regardless of whether the answers are right.

Borcherds told the student newspaper that he made the change after seeing many students use AI tools to earn top scores on their homework. Given that, he said, there was "no point" in paying readers to grade the work for correctness. He described the completion system as "not a very good system" but said he does not have a better alternative for now.

Borcherds received the Fields Medal, often described as the highest honor in mathematics, in 1998, according to the New York Post's account of the interview. The interview took place on Tuesday, October 20, and the story spread widely after it was shared on Hacker News and Slashdot on October 25.
A broader view of AI and mathematics

The interview followed OpenAI's announcement that its AI agents had apparently solved a version of the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the Millennium Prize problems. According to Science News, OpenAI announced the result on September 8, 2026, after running around 10,000 agents at a time. The proof was checked with the Lean verification tool, though mathematicians quoted by Science News said human review of the 166 page paper was still underway.

Borcherds told The Daily Californian he expects that within a few years AI will be able to do everything human mathematicians can do, and do it better. He said that five years ago mathematics was seen as one of the safest careers from the AI boom, and that he now does not know what to advise students considering research in the field. He added that when he asked ChatGPT, it also said it did not know what would happen.

He also predicted that academic inertia would keep the mathematics department largely unchanged for a couple of years, comparing it to printed academic journals, which he said have lacked a real purpose for about two decades. He compared the moment to earlier technologies that displaced human work, while noting that nothing like it had happened in mathematics before.
How Berkeley handles AI in courses

Anne Marie Richard, UC Berkeley's assistant vice provost for undergraduate education and chief academic technology officer, told The Daily Californian that the Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate asks faculty to include a statement on AI use in their course syllabi. AI policies vary widely by course level and subject, and each instructor decides the rules for their own class.

The campus has tested AI detection tools, including Turnitin and Rumi, and concluded they are not adequate for a campus wide standard, according to Richard. Berkeley's AI Hub, a directory of AI tools, training and policies, keeps a growing set of sample AI use statements that instructors can adapt for their syllabi.

NeuraFeed's reading: the decision is notable less for its scale, one professor's homework policy, than for who made it. A Fields Medal winner concluding that graded homework no longer measures what students know puts pressure on a basic tool of math teaching, and the lack of reliable detection leaves individual instructors to find their own answers.

Watch whether other UC Berkeley departments or the Academic Senate move from syllabus statements toward common rules, such as shifting more of the grade to in person exams, as AI tools keep improving at university level math.
